wrong_terms.text: The equation is: P = E/t (power = energy ÷ time).
wrong_terms.spec_term: power = (energy transferred)/time. The spec uses 'energy transferred', not 'energy'.

wrong_terms.text: One joule of work is done when a force of one newton moves an object one metre.
wrong_terms.spec_term: 'One joule of work is done when a force of one newton causes a displacement of one metre.' The spec uses 'displacement'.
'work done = force × distance moved along the line of action of the force'. The lesson gives the full phrase only in the next sentence, not in the bolded equation.

checkpoint_mismatch.checkpoint: 2: "A hairdryer has a power of 2000 W. How much energy does it transfer in 10 s?"
checkpoint_mismatch.why: The checkpoint tests the rearrangement E = Pt, which is taught in keyPoints[1] ("Rearrangements: E = Pt"). keyPoints[2] only lists typical power values ("Hairdryer: ~2000 W (2 kW).") and teaches no calculation. So the question does not test the key point it sits with.

checkpoint_mismatch.checkpoint: 1: correctFeedback "P = E/t = 18,000 ÷ 90 = 200 W. That is a sensible value for a runner."
checkpoint_mismatch.why: The feedback calls 200 W 'a sensible value for a runner'. The lesson's own figures in keyPoints[2].content give running as ~500–800 W, and the table gives walking as ~300 W. The lesson does not support the claim, and the student may be confused by the contradiction.

not_checked: All keyPoints have "diagram": null, so there were no diagrams or images to check.

examTips[2] "If a question gives you efficiency and power together, find the useful output power. It equals efficiency × input power." Efficiency is not in the supplied specification sections (4.1.1.4 and 4.5.2), so this could not be checked against spec text. It is physically correct only if efficiency is written as a decimal, not a percentage.

The everyday power values in keyPoints[2].content and tables[0] (for example "Human body at rest: ~80 W", "Walking: ~300 W", "Top sprinters may briefly reach 2000 W", "Electric car motor: 100–300 kW") and the historical claim "Steam engines could replace dozens of human workers by giving out many kilowatts non-stop" are not in the spec. They were checked only roughly against own knowledge, and they depend on whether metabolic or mechanical power is meant.
The spec skills references (MS 3b, c; MS 1c; WS 4.5) give no content to check the lesson against.
